utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Please continue, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milinic, yesterday we left off and we were talking about Directive 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And I'd ask for that to be put back in e-court. It's P00838, please. Can I have page 10 of the English and page 15 of the B/C/S. Thank you. And it's the last sentence that I wanted to examine again at the end of the first paragraph related to the Drina Corps. We talked about this yesterday and I just wanted to refer you to it again, the sentence which begins: "By planned and well thought out combat operations, create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." I want to go back to what you said in your statement about the convictions expressed in this document. Now, do you agree that what is stated here, the intentions expressed here, are odious and wrong in that sentence?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are not President Karadzic's convictions. They come from someone else's mind, and of course they're inappropriate and wrong. First of all, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that this is not a valid document. I doubt that it has the signature of President Karadzic. We have the stamp of the Main Staff --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We spoke about this yesterday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not discuss the stamp --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the stamp.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You can perhaps deal with it when you're questioned by the accused, but I'm not asking about the stamp. I'm asking you about the sentence. You said it's inappropriate. It's more than that, isn't it? It's hateful.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that the entire document is not valid. I don't want to discuss something that is not valid. It is not a valid document and these are not the words of President Karadzic. It is not a valid document. There is no sign, stamp, or protocol number that would be associated with the president of the republic. These are someone else's words and not President Karadzic's, clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. I'm not asking about stamps. I'm asking about what this says. What is imported by these words and I'm asking if you agree with me that it's hateful?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are talking about something abstract, about some words that are not the words of this man here. They are not his words and I cannot discuss them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Please, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're simply not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I want to read to you what Radovan Karadzic said to the RS Assembly in August 1995 regarding this directive.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wasn't going to ask for the document to be called up as it's been referred to on numerous occasions. It's P01412 and I'll just read it. It's the transcript from the 52nd Session of the RS Assembly dated the 6th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm going to read it to you. I'm going to read what is stated at page 111 to -12 of the English and of the B/C/S in e-court at page 95. Here it is: "The time had come and I signed Directive Number 7" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Also for the benefit of the interpreters, it's better for --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Better to show it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- for us to upload it. Yes, shall we --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Well, just to repeat, the relevant pages were English page 111 in e-court and B/C/S 95. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Kindly read slowly. Thank you. Interpreter's note: Could the Prosecutor please precisely indicate the passage in B/C/S that she's going to read in English for the purposes of translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, let me take you to e-court page 95. The passage begins six lines down from the top of the page, where it begins: "The time had come ...," so that's for the interpreters just to communicate what I'm reading there from the B/C/S. And in the English version, as I said, it's at page 112 -- sorry, 111 over to 112, starting at the bottom of the page in English, "the time had come..." So let me just read it, assuming that the interpreters have the relevant extract. "The time had come and I signed directive number 7 to capture Teocak, Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde. The directive was signed and we embarked on it" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do we have that passage in front of us?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, it should be -- my apologies, I should have located it for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Bottom of page 111, bottom paragraph in the middle of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Sorry, we cannot find the relevant passage in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Okay. It's at the top, it's six lines down from the top of the B/C/S, and it's --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, we have found it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And it's four lines up from the bottom of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let me just read it again. "The time had come and I signed directive number 7 to capture Teocak, Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde. The directive was signed and we embarked on it." And I'm just not going to read out the following couple of sentences. Turn over in the English, please, to 112, same page in the B/C/S. I'll pick it up. "I was in favour of all the decisions that we made and I support them. All the decisions are recorded in the Supreme Command. I ordered in verbal and written form to attack Zepa and Srebrenica. This is not fair, and the state cannot survive if we work without co-ordination and if rumours are spreading. None of these rumours are true in the essence. We are not able to take Gorazde at that time and we are still unable to conquer it because the threats are serious and we cannot afford to punch them in the eye right now, but there will be the right time to take Gorazde just as there was the right time to conquer Srebrenica. There will be the right time to attack and destroy Gorazde ..." Plain meaning of these words, Radovan Karadzic signed directive 7; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree. You can see that he says that he signed directive number 7 to take Teocak and Srebrenica and then he says it was all signed although he doesn't say it was signed by him. Then in the text he asked how come Tolimir shows such respect for the president of the republic? So this indicates again the rift between the civilian and military authorities, and then we have the words man, he wants you to become involved so that you cannot say that you were against it. Again, this clearly --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Stop, please.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- indicates the arguments between the military and political leadership, it's a quarrel.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You are deliberately distorting the plain meaning of this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand Serbian well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's an argumentative statement as opposed to a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It could of course be a question, but I think counsel can leave interpretation of words in these circumstances to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say that one needs to understand the sense in the Serbian language. You understand English, of course, but I can clearly see what it is in the Serbian language. It is the quarrel between the Main Staff and the political leadership, and the Main Staff was blaming the president because he was against it. I read between the lines in the Serbian, although you get it in English. I was in attendance during that session --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can we see the previous page?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, the previous page which was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me go back to the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes. That's 111 in the English. The B/C/S can stay on the same page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milinic, I don't follow what you just said. Here Mr. -- this is what Mr. Karadzic has said. Here he said: "The time had come and I signed directive number 7 ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't say "sign."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He did not say "sign," he said "signirati" which is one thing and to sign is a different thing. It was a matter of the arguments between the Main Staff and the president. They blamed him for halting combat activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you read out from "the time had come ..." aloud.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: If I can assist the witness, it's the beginning of the sixth line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just read out --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- the sentence aloud. "The time had come ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The time had come. I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: "Signirati" in the Serbian means to assign numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I did "signirati" to take Teocak and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And then the witness will need to repeat the quotation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [As read] "As for directive number 7 and it all, I assigned numbers to take Teocak and Srebrenica and Gorazde. It is all signed and we embarked on it. In the telegram you yourself describe it for the first time and I was surprised how come Tolimir showed such respect for the president of the republic" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I would request the CLSS to take a look at the passage and produce a report to the Chamber about this passage, in particular the -- with respect to "signirati."

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Perhaps I can move on to another RS Assembly Session, P01415. This is the transcript from the 54th Session of the RS Assembly dated 15/16 October 1995, and I'd ask to be shown up in e-court page 108 of the B/C/S and page 84 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: The passage in the English is at the bottom half of the third -- of the third full paragraph on the page, the paragraph that begins: "We must look at army publications ..." and then going down. I'm looking at the last sentence. And in the B/C/S it's the fifth paragraph down the page and it's just the last sentence of that paragraph. It's the penultimate paragraph on the page. And it's the last sentence of the penultimate paragraph. Have you found it, Mr. Milinic?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I am going to read out what I have as the English translation of this quote from Dr. Karadzic. "I have examined, approved, and signed seven directives. No one submitted the eighth and ninth to me ..." Have you found that in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So you'd agree there that Dr. Karadzic is stating that he signed seven directives; yes?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says; however, by the same token, it is clear that he was being set up by the army, that they did not even show him some things. They didn't show him what was to be signed. Now that I see it, it says the two directives were not even submitted to me for reading, let alone signing. Perhaps the seventh was treated the same way, maybe he was set up. The procedure was when I drafted something, I came to the president, and I would tell him what's in the document, and then he would say, "Okay," and he signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. But here is it true that this transcript says Mr. Karadzic signed seven directives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's true. That's what it says. However, being familiar with the situation I can tell you that I don't believe he signed it or perhaps he was set up and the seventh was slipped in to be signed alongside other documents. For me it is not a valid document because it does not contain certain elements that would have to be there had the president signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you look at the other things, you can see that there is always his signature and stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you explain what you meant by eight and ninth, Mr. Karadzic was set up by those two directives? Could you repeat what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He said that no one submitted the eighth and the ninth directive to him even for reading let alone signing. It was because General Gvero and the others drafted it and they decided who they wanted to listen to. He said that it was done without him, that General Gvero wrote it alone. Many things were imputed to the president. He was often given documents to sign without knowing what he was signing. The eighth and the ninth directive were not even submitted to him, and yet the army acted independently without the president of the republic in implementing them. That's key. That is what I was trying to point out. I was there day-in/day-out and I know what their relationship was. They were simply looking down upon the president of the republic. He was important -- unimportant to them, what he thought. If they wanted to set him up and submit a paper to him for signing, they would, and then they would say that it was a document by the president. There was a complete lack of -- there was a complete lack of respect and the president said so himself. They arranged for things to be signed --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and designed what they wanted to do. It was simply a group of military officers doing whatever they wanted and they used the president to sign what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. President, are you happy for me to move on from this section?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd like just to turn to another section in these minutes, please, and that's just finally at page 86 of the English and at page 111 of the B/C/S. And in the English it's the paragraph towards the bottom that starts: "As the supreme commander, I stood behind ..." And in the B/C/S we can see that paragraph, again about halfway down -- it's the last paragraph actually in the B/C/S. So you can see that, the last paragraph in the B/C/S. I'm going to read it.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: "As the supreme commander, I stood behind the plan for Zepa and Srebrenica, mainly for Srebrenica, Zepa was implied. Gentlemen, we would lose the war if there were 90 thousand armed Muslims in Zepa, we would lose the war. I personally supervised the plan without the knowledge of the Main Staff not even hiding anything but I happened to run into General Krstic and advised him to go straight into town" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Slow.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Sorry, my apologies. I'm going too fast.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: "... but I happened to run into General Krstic and advised him to go straight into town and to pronounce the fall of Srebrenica, and later we will chase the Turks around the woods. I approved an /?immediate/ task and a radical task and I don't regret it." Just confirm one thing for me, will you, this is October 1995. Can you confirm this for me, by months earlier, by August 1995, July/August 1995, the international press had reported allegations of mass killings of Muslim men and forced removal of thousands of elderly men, women, and children from Srebrenica? You can confirm that for me, can you?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. There was no forced removal. People asked to go to Tuzla, they wanted to go. What forcible removal? No one ordered anyone go. They said we wanted to go to our own to Tuzla. This is now Serb territory and we don't want to live here. They asked for the buses themselves to leave. Their requests were of that nature. What forcible removal? No one was forcibly removed. The people wanted to leave. No one wanted to be in another's territory. I did not want to live in Mostar because it was a Croat and Muslim town. I'm a refugee as well. [In English] I'm a refugee, too. I don't want to live with Muslims and Croats who are armed. Yes. [Interpretation] Who are armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mass killings, do you agree now that Muslim men were killed on a mass scale after the fall of Srebrenica? Do you accept that now?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way. No way. I am witness to it. I received from the state security this many papers, 15.000 Muslims left the encirclement in Srebrenica. They went through, through the Serb army. They reached Zvornik and wanted to torch it. It was without the Serb army and whatever little soldiers there were left opened fire on the Muslims. At that moment through a loud-speaker Tursunovic, the Muslim leader, said, "Dear Serbs, only let us go through Tuzla. Unless you do so, there are 15.000 of us who will torch Zvornik town, we'll destroy it unless you let us through ..." and they were --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- let through by Zvornik, 15.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Do you not accept now that thousands of Muslim men were killed following the fall of Srebrenica by Bosnian Serb forces? Do you not accept that?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, I don't. That is incorrect. It was set up by the Muslim media and by different world factors. That had not been done. Perhaps I can acknowledge that there were cases of perhaps a few hundred, but they were all killed in combat. They passed by Zvornik, the 15.000. I personally talked to some people. We had our line towards Tuzla and they attacked this line to break through to Tuzla. They attacked from behind, and several thousand Muslims were killed in combat. I talked to a man who said I had a machine-gun, I was firing and wave upon wave of people were falling down. 40 Serbs were killed but they broke through, whereas thousands of dead Muslims were left dead. Later on, it was said that they were executed, but they were killed in combat. Perhaps a few, a few hundred were executed, but most of them were killed in combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You accept that at the time it's not just the Muslim media so-called but the international press and international actors were reporting allegations of the forced displacement of thousands of individuals and the fear that thousands had been killed? This is in July.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Muslim propaganda. Alija Izetbegovic personally planned an operation to blame the Serbs and to have NATO bomb the Serbs. He wanted to use their own casualties. The Islamic jihad is such that they will sacrifice thousands of their people for their goals without any problems. At the time we didn't know what jihad is. Now you know what jihad is. In Baghdad you plant a bomb, kill 50 people, and nothing happens. It's water under the bridge. Alija Izetbegovic kills his own people in order to blame the Serbs. He -- these 100 people don't mean anything to him, but the Serbs will be seen as criminals by the international community. Srebrenica is a huge set up. I tell you, people were killed in combat. Maybe a few hundred were executed, there may have been such cases. I learned of them subsequently, that there were some groups of extreme Serbs who did something of that kind, but those were a couple of hundred. But most of them were killed in the break through. 15.000 men, you can't do --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- anything to stop that. They keep assaulting, you mow them down and they keep coming.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I just want to turn to one document, please, 65 ter 13645. I just want to quickly show you one document that was sent to Dr. Karadzic on the 24th of July, 1995. It's only available in English. This is the cover sheet indicating that a letter was transmitted to Dr. Karadzic, and I would just ask, please, to go to the third page which is clearer than the fax copy on the second page. There is the letter itself. There's a letter from the Special Rapporteur of the Commission for Human Rights, 24th of July, 1995. And just in the first paragraph there I'll read it so you can have it translated. "I would like to express my deepest concern regarding the recent events in the Srebrenica area which resulted in the forced displacement of some 40.000 individuals. It has been reported that as a result of these events several thousand individuals are unaccounted for and there is fear that many of these have either been killed or detained." Now, presumably these were allegations coming from international actors about which you were aware in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm asking you if you were aware of these allegations coming from international actors in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't follow the documents of international organisations. I focused on the documents of our security services and I trusted these, because international propaganda at the time was unanimously oriented against the Serbs. It says here "forced displacement," but it wasn't force. The people wanted to go; it was their free will. People wanted to go from Bijeljina, a Serbian town where nobody exerted pressure on them, nothing was happening to them, and the president who was concerned. Why do the people want to move? And I was a member of the commission to -- that spoke to those people to investigate that. Is anybody doing anything to you? And they replied, "No, but we don't want to live in a country where there is a war. We want to go to Australia, Canada, and other countries. We'll be grateful if you let us go." And we did receive letters of gratitude from those who did leave. And imagine Srebrenica, a town where the Serbian army had just entered. They had lived in fear of the Serbs for years and everybody wants to leave to go to a safe territory. They were calling it the free territory where the Muslims were, whereas the Serbs called the territory where the Serbs were free territory. It was a war. Everybody wants to get away from war. The people wanted to move of their own will and go to their territory. I was a witness to that. I talked to people in such towns such as Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I didn't follow the documents of international organisations, you didn't follow these documents, these sorts of allegations, did you, because you knew about the killings already. It was no news to you, was it?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't know. I had reports of state security and military security saying that 15.000 Muslims had gone through our lines and that intense fighting was going on because they were trying to break through toward Tuzla. Those were the real reports and I monitored those reports. I was an intelligence man. I read reports from the field and I wasn't interested in the jabber of the international community because they were against us anyway, you know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Let's turn to the DB, shall we, the state security --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said -- what he said, the president was concerned why -- [in English] president was concerned why those people want to leave. [Interpretation] And then he said the president established and sent a commission to talk to them and I was a member of that commission.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. There was a commission with five members --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that spoke to those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do not overlap with the interpretation, please. What page, what line, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 15, page 15, line 9. Before "and I was a member of that commission." Before that sentence he said the president established a commission and sent it out to speak to those people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- there was a commission comprising five people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are dealing with the transcript. Please continue, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I don't think that Mr. Tieger has informed Ms. Pack that we're supposed to ask for time when we run out, so the Prosecution has, as I understand it, used up the time allotted for cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you leave it to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: She's now about to conclude her cross-examination. That's why I left her to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. But by doing that, you don't allow us to be heard. So we would prefer if a system like we had with Dr. Karadzic when he did his direct examinations -- when he did his cross-examinations, that you were telling him how much time he had left and then he had to comply with that and the Prosecution can be heard. So we would like the opportunity to be heard rather than the time just expiring and not being able to be heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber is following the situation, so you may rest assured. And please leave it to the Chamber. Yes, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. President. I had thought I had about 12 minutes more, allowing for time for objections and arguments yesterday, but perhaps my estimation of the time is incorrect so that's why I hadn't asked yet for more time. I was hoping to be able to conclude in the next 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I will -- I wanted to leave it at that, but you may go back to the Prosecution case and without asking leave the Chamber granted Mr. Karadzic a lot of more time at the end of his cross-examinations. I'm confident there were so many cases. Let's continue. Let me see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You don't disagree, do you, that there were DB operatives active on the ground in the Srebrenica area during the Srebrenica operations including before and after the fall of Srebrenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Srebrenica at that moment was a combat zone where the military decides about everything. It decides who can go there and who cannot. It was very difficult. We even had a problem there between state security and the military leadership. I can tell you --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'd just like to ask you to answer my question, please. Do you deny that there were DB operatives working and active in the Srebrenica area both before and after its fall?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The state security had its collaborators even among the Muslims. You know that operatives and collaborators can be found in the ranks of the other side too, but then work was difficult, their access was difficult because the military had control over any movement, and there was a clash between security and the Main Staff. And I want to tell you about it. An operative of state security informs General Mladic --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- why not? Why not? You asked me about operatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: You can deal with this in re-examination. I'm going to ask you a further question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can we have up, please, P04974.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: So is it your evidence that there were no DB operatives in Potocari, working in Potocari, on the 12th of July --

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: On the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was off limits. The military declared it off limits. Operatives of state security are civilians. It was a restricted area. You know what that is, combat zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can you look at the document, please, on the screen. This is a document that is signed by Dragan Kijac, head of the RDB. You're familiar with him, obviously; is that right? You know who Dragan Kijac is?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew everybody, not just him. I know everybody in the RS. Of course I knew him. I knew everything. Now I know even you. When they asked me to know -- do you know Milica? I would say yes. And I will tell you why these people were rewarded and you interrupted me --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can you just -- let's just for the record, this is a communication from Kijac, a proposal to the deputy minister of the interior, that number of members thereafter identified of the RDB Bijeljina CRDB, that's the state security department centre, are awarded money for their extraordinary contribution and engagement during the liberation of Zepa and Srebrenica. And it lists there a number of members of the Zvornik DB, yes, and the Bijeljina CRDB. Do you agree that those are the individuals who are listed there? They include Sinisa Glogovac, Mile Renovica, who is the head of the Zvornik DB. Do you agree that all those are members of the DB in Zvornik and Bijeljina, yes?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to tell you. These people were rewarded because they discovered that 15.000 Muslims broke through the encirclement of the Serbian army and they informed General Mladic, saying, "General, here you are, 15 [as interpreted] people went through, they will burn down Zvornik, they will make it to Tuzla." General Mladic simply waved his hand and said, "Well, let them go. Go on, send 20 people to find those 15.000 of theirs." General Mladic didn't believe that 15.000 fighters went through our lines, made it through our lines. These seven people found that out. They are from Zvornik and they saw that these 70 [as interpreted] thousand passed through. They said, "Send out your troops because they will burn down Zvornik." Mile Renovica is from Zvornik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, just a second. If you could bear with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, shall we continue? But, Mr. Robinson, the Chamber considered your observation again and then -- and your observation, I have to say, was not a correct one. As long as I remember, the Chamber has never limited Mr. Karadzic's cross-examination when his line of cross-examination was relevant; in particular, we considered in this witness's case the way the question and answer was proceeding. So the Chamber finds that some extension was appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, actually, Mr. President, I completely agree, and I wouldn't have objected to an extension in this particular case. My point was a different one. My point was that during the Prosecution's case when Dr. Karadzic had a time-limit, he was told that he had five minutes left or two minutes left --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When the line of his cross-examination goes beyond the relevant -- the point, that -- the Chamber often asked him as a way of warning, asked him how much longer he would need --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- but we didn't -- the Chamber didn't do that as long as he remains on the relevant part. That's the policy I had taken. Shall we leave it there?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I did think I had 56 minutes left for this morning -- not now but when I started, so perhaps if I just wrap up in the next few minutes. My apologies if I have gone over the time but I had actually thought I'd kept within it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'll ask you to look at one more document, please. Can we have P04388 on the screen, please. Now I think you've testified -- you certainly said it in your witness statement that you got all of the communications from the VRS Main Staff sector for intelligence and security; is that right? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was getting compilations made by the intelligence service about the situation in the field, where the Muslim forces were moving, what was currently happening with the Croatian forces. So that was a compilation or a daily digest that I received about what the spies or the intelligence operatives of the RS were learning on the ground. I informed the president about what he needed to know. I never mentioned trifles to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This is a communication, isn't it, from Popovic, Lieutenant-Colonel Vujadin Popovic. It's dated the 12th of July, he's the Drina Corps security officer, to the Main Staff sector for OB. The time recorded on it is 1730 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask for the English, please, to be shown on page 2 of the English, please, in e-court and it can remain on page 1 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: He's reporting on the course of the day. And at paragraph 3, I'd like to read out what he says there. He says: "A refugee group of about 30.000 - 35.000 women, children, elderly, the infirm, and the sick is located after beyond the UNPROFOR base towards Srebrenica ..." et cetera, it goes on. And then I'll pick up, please, at the last two sentences: "We are separating men from 17 - 60 years of age and we are not transporting them. We have about 70 of them so far and the security organs and the DB are working with them." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, but I haven't seen this letter before. This was sent to the Supreme Command, that is, the president of the republic. We never received this communication. We only received daily compilations. This wasn't part of it. I have never seen this letter before. I don't know. I cannot comment what this is about because I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Well, you can see now it is a report the DB are working with the VRS security organs -- they're working together on the ground in Potocari with the separated Muslim men --

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they never worked together. I mean state security and the security organs. There was always a clash between the two. There was state security and military security. They were not on good terms. There were also rivalries between brigade commanders and civilian municipal authorities. I don't think that state security organs were involved in this. It functioned very poorly. I told you already what it was like when the state security informed General Mladic about events. He didn't -- of which he didn't get information from the field. They -- he didn't believe them. He sent out 20 people to find 15.000. I don't believe that this happened. We never received such reports from state security, nor did we get any from the military security. They mostly gave us information about the enemy, where enemy troops are concentrated, what kind of combat activity can be expected, and so on. I doubt that they worked together.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: It's just not true, is it. You --

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And I'm not going to refer to another document because I know my time is up.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: But you have referred in your statement to a log-book, P02989, to a log-book that records daily communications on the 11th, on the 12th, on the 13th, on the 14th, on the 15th, daily communications from the RS Main Staff OB to the president, to the RS MUP DB, and to the RS defence ministry, timed at around the same time, early in the morning, every day --

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it. Yes. These are the daily compilations I mentioned to you. The Main Staff, that is, the intelligence sector would send us a daily compilation containing the positions of the enemy units, what their intentions were, where an attack can be expected. I told you that we received those all the time, but they never mentioned such things. We never learned of such things, no, we didn't get this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: We don't have these documents, do we, the documents referred to in your log-book, because they're missing, is that right? They're missing.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How should I know what you have? You had access to everything. In 1995/1996, you were able to copy everything. I saw you walking up and down the hallways of the facilities of the president of the republic. I really can have no way of knowing what you did copy and what you didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I realise I'm at the end of my time. No more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pack. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency. I'll try to be as brief as possible and I'll start with the latest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ambassador, you were asked just now about documents, where these documents were, the ones that came from the Main Staff. Does the Main Staff keep copies of the documents they send me?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, certainly, they have an obligation to do that. Nothing can be sent without having a copy kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we sent -- we are sending a document, do we leave copies too? So does the sending and receiving party have a copy of the document?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. That's an obligation too. That's why I was upset because one document was not prescribed, it was not proper, rather. Every document has to have a letter-head of the president and also this number, strictly confidential, your signature, and a stamp and seal of the president of the republic. That would be the right kind of document. One copy remains in our hands and the other one is sent to the receiving party, and that is why I complained about that directive because allegedly that is your signature but you're not to the Main Staff, you're the Supreme Command, you're the president of the republic. And this document was not registered in the archives of the president of the republic, and it is not in the military office of the president and it is not registered as strictly confidential. I do not find such documents to be valid. What is valid is what is properly registered. One copy is sent to the receiving party and another copy is archived properly, signed, stamped with the seal of the president of the republic. Those are real, valid documents.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness is speaking at a pace which is too fast for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. If you are speaking so fast, it will not be reflected in the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- transcript correctly. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 108, Prosecution Exhibit P1415, this is a transcript of a session of the National Assembly. It says there -- actually, it was read out to you, it was shown to you. I'll read out the entire paragraph. "Gentlemen, we need to look at our military lists and you will see why" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have a copy of this text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, for the benefit of the correct translation, we need to upload it. Please wait.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the second paragraph. In English it's page 84. It's the beginning of the second, or rather, third paragraph in English, "We must look ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is what it says: "We must look at army publications, our army journals, and you'll see why, or that which went down in the trenches, and you'll see why, or what General Gvero is writing in Novosti at the moment when we are losing large pieces of the Krajina, what he found most urgent to say, that's not for the Assembly, that's between me and him, but, gentlemen, I have examined, approved, and signed seven directives. No one submitted the eighth and ninth ones to me ..." and so on and so forth. First of all, could you please explain the following to me. What does it mean when you say "signirati" and what does it mean when you say "potpisati," "sign"?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Signirati" means send to someone, I mean forward to someone, forward, that's what it actually means; whereas, to sign "potpisati," is to sign [In English] "potpisati" is to sign. To sign is "potpisati." [Interpretation] That is the difference between the Serbian and English language, whereas "signirati" in Serbian means to forward or write something, that's not signing at all. In Serbian that does not mean to sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What word is used here, "signirati" or "potpisati" when he said he signed seven directives?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will get to that, but it says "signiro" whereas in this paragraph it says "potpisati," but in that paragraph that only has to do with number 7 it says "signirati," meaning "forwarded," "marked." Page 95, this document, P1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, I remember that it -- in the 52nd Session which is Exhibit P1412, that that passage used the so-called "signirati," but here what's the term used? Is it "signirati" or "potpisati," Mr. Milinic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it says "potpisati," signed, here, but this generally pertains to some seven directives --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that was my question. You answered the question. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. D232, directive number 1, could we please have that in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In terms of the register or the letter-head -- no, P232 -- no, that shouldn't be it. It's D, not P, Defence. Yes. May I kindly ask you to look at the top of the page and see who it was that wrote this?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and their numbers are there, strictly confidential number such and such. And this was compiled by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please take a look at the last page so that we see who signed it.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The signatory is commander Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic. This is a typical military document of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D593, could we now please take a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The same question, please, could you take a look --

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Likewise, up here it says the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, their strictly confidential number, and this would have to be a document of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's 02, like the previous one; right?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 02.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the last page now please be displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who signed this other directive?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Likewise, commander, Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic, that is to say the commander of the Main Staff. This is a military document, a typical military document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D235, could we please have that, Defence 235.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, again, could you identify where this was created, which institution this is, and who signed it? We'll see that at the end.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Likewise, the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, their strictly confidential number, and therefore this is a document of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have page 13 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Likewise, signed by the commander Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic. Likewise, this is a directive of the Main Staff and the signatory is Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic. This is a proper document, a proper military document of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P976, that's a Prosecution document, Prosecution, P, could we please take a look at that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, where was this document created?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, their strictly confidential number, so this is also a document of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, a directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which number?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Strictly confidential 02/5-216.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the number of the directive?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The directive is number 4, that is directive number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Signed by commander Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic, that is to say General Mladic signed directives. You did not sign the seventh directive. It was Ratko Mladic who signed it. I have seen several directives now and they were all signed by Ratko Mladic. That is why I could not accept that you had signed that document. All directives were signed by General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 1866, could we please take a look at that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where this document was created and whose stamp it bears?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and it bears the stamp of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. Again, this is an excerpt from a directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the penultimate page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Signed by the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic, directive properly signed, a proper military document with the stamp of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. That's what I've been saying all the time. General Mladic signed directives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D3688. And for the record, Your Honours, 65 ter number 22049 which was on the 92 ter notification is in fact Exhibit P3149. So to avoid duplication, this will be substituted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. P977, this is a Prosecution document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When was this document created and what is this document, which directive?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is also directive number 5, the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, strictly confidential number 02/2-479. This is a document of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, directive number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the penultimate page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Signed by commander Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have Prosecution number P3039.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is this? Can you tell us? And can you tell us where this was created?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directive number 6, but this time -- well, it's also a document of the Main Staff, but it says strictly confidential number 02/2-934, but it no longer says the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, but what they wrote was the Supreme Command of the armed forces of Republika Srpska. But no, this is a document of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. That is as clear as day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the -- all the signs there, everything you can see there, all the designations, the register, all of that is from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milinic, the interpreters were not able to hear you. Could you repeat slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is a document that was created at the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. This was not written in the Presidency of Republika Srpska, or rather, at the military office at the Supreme Command. There is no number there, there is no number of the register of the Supreme Command, or rather, the president of the republic, 02/2 are the numbers according to the register. This is the Main Staff, this is their number, and up here what is written is the Supreme Command. To a degree this may be considered a forgery. Supreme Command, that has to contain the letter-head of the president of the republic. It has to be on his writing paper. And also, all the designations have to be those of the president of the republic. I find this to be a suspicious document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have established where it was created. Let us see where it was signed.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, yes, how come Radovan Karadzic's signature is here? How come Radovan Karadzic's signature is here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whose stamp this is?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The stamp is that of the president of the republic, yes. The stamp is that of the president of the republic. And that is what gives it validity. When your signature is there and your stamp is there, then -- yes, I could acknowledge this document because it has the seal of the president of the republic and the signature of Radovan Karadzic. It is not quite proper, but I can recognise it, acknowledge it, because of the seal, the seal of the president of the republic has been affixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We've seen number 7, we've shown you directive number 7 -- oh, we don't have to call that up again. So, Mr. Ambassador, was I precise when I know I said that I signed seven directives, and out of these seven directives how many did I actually sign?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of all seven, I can only recognise this one as having been signed by you because it has your signature and your seal, the seal of the president of the republic. And also your signature, Radovan Karadzic, president, your signature -- so this is the only directive that you signed, not the rest. On the rest of them there is no stamp of yours, no letter-head, no register number that belongs to you. I would only recognise this one, although this one has certain shortcomings because it has not been registered in our office. It does have these shortcomings but I would recognise it because it has your seal affixed to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether you have assessed what led me to say that I signed seven directives, although I had not signed them? What kind of atmosphere was this?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was much division between the Main Staff and the president of the republic. You were always in favour of unity. You always strove to say that you worked jointly so that the people would not be familiar with the rift. Throughout the rift we tried to hide it. We -- you tried to undertake measures and change the military leadership. We tried not to cause any divisions among the people and that is why you said that the directives have been accepted as a result of some kind of joint work in order not to cause divisions among the people. Throughout the period you worked actively on your attempts in order to try and change the military leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we next have P1412, page 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This has already been shown to you. I think it's page 111 in English. Perhaps not. We'll see. It's 111. Was this session full of arguments and quarrels? Perhaps you can remind yourself if you read it briefly.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do kindly remind me of the date of this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 6th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, yes. It was in the situation where you dismissed the commander of the Main Staff. On the 6th of August, 1995, the chief of the -- the commander of the Main Staff, Ratko Mladic, had already been dismissed, and this is the situation in which this discussion developed. You had the support of the people's Assembly, whereas all of the generals immediately launched a boycott. They said they would boycott you and the red government you represented. There was a general -- an uprising of generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 6th of August was there any knowledge of any illegal killings that the deputies may have been aware of or that the government may have been aware of, at least the people you talked to? Was there any kind of information available save for much rumour in the media?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one sent any kind of information of any killings. I only received information about combat and the break through I discussed when the 15.000 Muslims broke through Zvornik to Tuzla, and I discussed that great clash. No military or state security report mentioned any kind of killing. To date I still do not believe it took place. It is all part of this massive Muslim propaganda. When I was at an out-of-country voting centre in Vienna, I found 1.000 Srebrenica Muslims who registered to vote, and yet back home they were on the burial list in Srebrenica. I intervened and the 1.000 votes were then checked because people could not vote if they were dead. I caused much discontent in the out-of-country voting centre in Vienna. The Srebrenica graveyard is one big farce. There -- it contains the bodies of people who died of natural causes in 1992, 1993, and yet all of them were buried as war victims. The Serbs were set up with the whole thing. I will never acknowledge it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What elections are you talking about, the ones in 1996?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1996, 1997, and 1998. We kept having these rounds of elections and I was constantly in Vienna for months at a time as a representative of the RS government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back to P1451, page 108 and 84 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could you maybe repeat the number, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably 1415.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yeah. [Interpretation] Page 84 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at the part before "military publications." It says: "Gentlemen, this is destroying the state ..." And then the next sentence: It suffices that I lost my confidence in several generals because I felt it on my own skin and the skin of these people, and in their media I could see that they were working against the state as of day one. And if I need to explain why we thanked General Gvero, because that is the formulation, we thank him because he has both merits and effect and he worked hard ... Do you recall that I objected to their work for three and a half years? Since day one I resisted their concept of how they saw the state and the army.

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I've already said, you say here that you lost confidence in several generals and that you could feel it on your own skin and the skin of the people. They did not listen to you at all. You were just a figurehead, and yet you tried to change things all the time, you kept working on their removal. But it was a sort of general junta and they rallied together. If you touch one of them, it's touching all of them, they are immediately against you, wanting to cause trouble, and they had the force, they had the weapons. Yesterday I said that it was stated at the Assembly session that General Novak in front of a line of soldiers said that Radovan Karadzic is not our commander, the president of the republic is not our commander. Their ambition was to gain civilian power as well, to have it all for themselves. They kept asking for a state of war to be proclaimed so that they could be the main in command. And the heads of municipality could never agree with commanders of brigades because the commanders wanted to have everything. In the West they are controlled by civilians, but in a state of war -- actually, in the war itself, they thought they were gods and that they could not be touched. They basically decided on everything and yet you tried to have them removed. In the trenches they distributed leaflets and brochures against you. Throughout I could see that things were not functioning properly. The civilian authorities had no control and attempts were made to regain that control but it couldn't be. This misfortune of General Gvero was a member of the JUL party, Mira Markovic's party, kept putting forth different kinds of ideology.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could Mr. Karadzic kindly please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please repeat your question. You overlapped with the interpretation of the answer. Could you start over, all over again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last question: Let's look at what the ambassador discussed when he mentioned a senior officer who denied my confidence. It is P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, the Chamber has to rise now. We'll have a break for half an hour --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I can conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have to rise, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, you said that you did not see individual documents of the military security service, but rather compilations of material. Can you tell us who produced them and sent them to the president's office?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such compilations of documents were put together by the sector for intelligence and security at the Main Staff of the VRS. It was General Tolimir who was the head and there was General -- no, actually, Colonel Salapura and Colonel Beara. They were the three people at the helm and one of the three always signed the document which would then be sent to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we next have P970, page 95. We can see my contribution begin. In English that's page 95. P970.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It has to do with what you said that at the Assembly session there was discussion of a senior officer who said that I was not his supreme commander and that I was unimportant. Can we have that?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember General Bozo Novak. Apparently he said that in front of a line of around 1.000 soldiers and that is how it was interpreted at the Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If we don't have it, I can read it out from hard copy page 102. I'll read it out in English and then we'll have it interpreted. [In English] Here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be coming. For the sake of having correct interpretation, we better have it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is not the right number. I asked for P970, page 95. That's where I begin. Can we see that in English. Yes, it's fine in English. Next can we go to page 102 in English, please. And then we should go to the Serb page where it begins "the report clearly demonstrates ..." The Serb version begins at page 98 and then six pages over -- oh, no it's page 86 in e-court in the Serbian. Let me just find where it is. "A senior officer ..." It begins with "simply" or "simply put." Here in this place a senior officer who was awarded his rank by me said that the supreme commander of his is not Karadzic, Karadzic is unimportant. But the office that Karadzic holds does matter and must be respected. And on the morrow some other Karadzic will be there. You cannot expect one to say this will be - if you'll pardon the expression - I don't know what kind of state. This is a priestly, clerical, Chetnik, capitalist, this or that kind of state. And then further below: "The report clearly demonstrates a total disrespect of the ministry," that's the next paragraph "and the minister. We can't have that." And then further below: "The army is not and cannot be a structure above the state, but it is a state organ ..." Mr. Ambassador, you were a military intelligence man before the war. Can you tell us whether you were able to establish the basis for these conceptual differences between civilian authorities and military structures? Was it ideological? Was it some kind of foreign influence or was it a struggle for power? What was it?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer the question, we lost the e-court again. Yes, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I object. This isn't something that was -- arises from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think throughout there were stories of differences between the armed forces and civilian structures, and now I'm trying to discuss the basis of those disagreements. And this witness is certainly in a position to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us then as an officer and intelligence man what was the basis, what factors or combination of factors, were the cause of this permanent disagreement?

utterances.speaker: GORDAN MILINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was this permanent disagreement because the generals believed in another ideology, they used to be JNA generals, mostly communists who could not navigate the democratic changes and multi-party elections. Many of them were members of the League of Communists. There were also members of Mira Markovic's party, but there was another factor which played a decisive role which was particularly pronounced when Serbia imposed sanctions on the RS. Not a single civilian leader could go to Serbia as of August 1994 when Serbia imposed the sanctions on the RS. Any general could cross the border and military personnel regularly went this way or that. The centre of power, the centre of decision-making for the generals was not in Pale, it was somewhere else. I have to tell you that many people from the field told me that General Mladic keeps repeating that: My command is not in Pale. I listen to no one in Pale. That is what people from the field kept telling me. So there were different reasons, ideological, their membership of other parties, their lack of knowledge about their own people because the fighters in the trenches had completely different views than theirs. And in this general elite there were other ideas in circulation and probably other goals too. I suspect they wanted to seize power all together, but they couldn't because they would be seen as a general junta. They would not have been recognised as leadership, not as long as there was the president of the republic and the Assembly because they were democratically elected in 1990 during elections. They were cautious of it and occasionally they would listen to a thing or two, but mostly --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all background noise be stopped.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that was the basis of our misunderstandings. Those people simply could not navigate the multi-party system and they belonged and believed in other goals and ideas. Of course they also had desire to rule. They wanted to obtain civilian power as well. I know General Mladic said several times that he would like to be the president of the RS. I heard it several times --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Shall we pause there. Yes. Probably I was mistaken. Ms. Pack, did you deal with the so-called rift between the political leaders and military leaders?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No, no, that was the reason why I objected to this. This isn't something that arose out of my cross-examination. It's re-examination-in-chief. There was a long soliloquy about this topic at the beginning of examination-in-chief, and this is it. This is a second --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mladic's words are quoted here of him giving up political ambitions. What do you mean this wasn't raised in the cross-examination? It was challenged. I'm convinced that it was raised but I can't find the page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Anyway, thank you, Ambassador. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milinic, could you tell us again what your incumbent job is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm currently a professional diplomat of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm a minister councillor with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Milinic. I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could call your next witness, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we're ready to have the testimony of Nedjo Nikolic. He's here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, may I just ask for a couple of minutes for the Prosecution to change seats, for me to change seats with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Good morning, Mr. Nikolic. Before you commence your evidence, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of procedure and evidence that we have here at the international Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Nikolic. I kindly ask you to speak slowly and to pause between question and answer so as to enable the interpreters to interpret everything that was said. Did you give a statement to my Defence team, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see 1D09601.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the screen before you. Do you see that statement of yours on the screen?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see my statement on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read and sign that statement?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I read and signed this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the witness the last page for him to identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: NEDJO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This statement faithfully reflects all that I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
